deep.reconstruction:
The page is a heavily overwritten pencil draft on the back of a printed postal form (columns No., Auslage, Porto, Franko). Most of it is illegible. Only a few words and symbols can be read with confidence: 'Da die Curven a_1, a_2, ..., a_n' (written twice, the first attempt struck out), 'a_1, a_2', several isolated 'a_1', '1 ... 1' or '2-1' (probably an index count such as n-1), 'Querschnitt', 'Die Fläche ...', '... durch den Querschnitt ... zerfällt', and 'Querschnitte'.

Context: the previous page (157r) treats the integral ∫(X dx + Y dy) of a complete (exact) differential on a surface. It discusses how the integral is continued from a curve and how its values on the two sides of a cut differ by a constant. This page continues with the analysis-situs part of the same argument. It is evidently a draft of §1 ('Lehrsätze aus der analysis situs') of Riemann's 'Theorie der Abel'schen Functionen' (Crelle 54, 1857); compare also the 1851 dissertation, §§6-7.

My reconstruction of the intended content (not legible verbatim; inferred from the keywords and the published parallel):

(1) Additivity of boundaries. Suppose a system of closed curves a_1, ..., a_n together completely bounds a piece of the surface F. Suppose also that a_1, ..., a_{n-1} together with a curve b bound a piece. Then a_n and b together bound a piece. In modern terms: boundaries form a subgroup, and homology with Z/2 coefficients is well defined.

(2) Connectivity. F is called (m+1)-fold connected if m closed curves can be drawn on it that neither singly nor together bound a piece, while every further closed curve bounds together with some of them. The same order is reached via cross-cuts (Querschnitte), i.e. cuts running from boundary to boundary. A cross-cut that does not disconnect F lowers the order of connection by 1. A cross-cut that splits ('zerfällt') F into two pieces of orders m1 and m2 satisfies m1 + m2 = m + 1. After a sequence of cross-cuts F is reduced to simply connected pieces, which yields the invariance of the connectivity number.

(3) Application to the integral. On a surface made simply connected by cross-cuts, the integral of a complete differential is single-valued. Its jumps across the cuts are constant along each cut.

No explicit computation can be reconstructed beyond this.
errors: No errors can be assessed. The text is mostly illegible and the legible fragments match Riemann's published, correct statements on connectivity.

results.what: If curve systems a_1..a_n and a_1..a_{n-1},b each bound a piece of the surface, then a_n together with b bounds a piece (additivity of boundaries).
results.modern_name: Homology relations / boundaries form a group (mod 2 homology)

results.what: Order of connection of a surface and its change under cross-cuts (Querschnitte): reduction by one, or splitting with m1+m2=m+1.
results.modern_name: Riemann's connectivity number (first Betti number + 1), cut-reduction invariance

results.what: The integral of an exact differential is single-valued on the cut surface, with constant jumps across the cuts.
results.modern_name: Periods of closed 1-forms / monodromy of abelian integrals

deep.surprise_reason: This appears to be a working draft of the published analysis-situs lemmas of the 1857 Abelian functions paper. The material is well known as Riemann's; at most it is of minor interest as draft evidence.

checkable.asserts: A non-separating cross-cut lowers the connectivity order m by 1 (a trivial bookkeeping identity).
A closed surface of genus p, once punctured (one boundary), is (2p+1)-fold connected: it needs 2p cross-cuts to become simply connected (order 1).

checkable.sympy: m,m1,m2=symbols('m m1 m2'); solve(Eq(m1+m2, m+1), m2)
checkable.asserts: Riemann's relation for a separating cross-cut: the orders of the two pieces sum to m+1.
The Euler characteristic 1-2p of the punctured genus-p surface equals 2 - connectivity order (2p+1), consistent with connectivity = 2 - chi.

Near the middle-left, '2-1' (or 'n-1') appears as an index count rather than '1 ... 1'.
The phrase '... durch den Querschnitt ... zerfällt' likely belongs to the statement that a cross-cut divides the surface into pieces. It parallels the published wording in Crelle 54, §1.
